title: Resilient Sovereign Power: Overview
lede: Kronos studies how a compact fusion generator could supply resilient, self-sufficient power to fixed defense installations, and states plainly the gates that stand between design and hardware.
body: What resilient sovereign power means here

For a defense installation, resilient sovereign power is the ability to generate the electricity a mission needs on-site, without depending on a commercial grid, a fuel convoy, or a foreign supply chain, and to keep generating through disruption. Kronos studies whether the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) — a D–3He tandem-mirror generator using direct energy conversion — could serve that role at fixed installations (bases and fixed forward sites, not naval platforms).

This is a design-and-simulation study, not deployed hardware. The breeder (Hyperion) construction begins Q2 2027 with first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium targeted around 2030; the burner is a later, harder machine. We claim no hardware net gain before FOAK, and none at all for the burner today.
Candor is part of the value. Four physics gates presently separate the burner from a fieldable sovereign power source, and every one is a design finding, not a marketing caveat:
Plug coil overstressed roughly 3–3.9× at the design bore — infeasible as specified.
Plug operating regime sits 166–830× beyond any device ever run — not post-dictable today.
Helium-3 fuel demand runs ~400× domestic supply per commercial unit — the fuel does not exist at terrestrial scale.
Availability of ~0.86–0.995 versus hyperscale Tier III 0.99982 — 30–100× short on downtime.

These gates are why the breeder (which breeds tritium and helium-3) and lunar helium-3 matter, and why any near-term architecture treats fusion as one hardened element in a redundant power system — never a sole source. The pages in this section develop each theme with full physics candor.

Each page pairs a specific capability — islanding, black-start, survivability, low signature — with the honest engineering reality behind it. Where a page touches the burner, it repeats the relevant gate so no capability is read in isolation from its precondition. The consistent message is that resilient sovereign power is a system outcome: a hardened, redundant, sovereignly fuelled architecture in which a mature burner would be the anchor, achievable today only in design and simulation.

title: Why Fixed Installations, Not Naval
lede: The burner in its Aegis housing is scoped to fixed defense installations; naval propulsion is explicitly out of scope for the design as studied.
body: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is studied only for fixed installations — main operating bases, fixed forward sites, and (in the MetroVolt housing) data centers. The Aegis housing is a fixed defense installation generator. It is not a naval power plant, and shipboard or submarine propulsion is not part of the design as studied.

Why the boundary is drawn there

A tandem-mirror generator is a large, magnetically complex machine with a 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat fields. Its mass, shielding, and cryogenic infrastructure suit a prepared, fixed foundation far better than a moving hull. Fixing the site also lets the design assume a hardened, surveyed emplacement with room for redundancy and shielding — assumptions that a ship cannot make.

Fixing the installation does not remove the honest gates. Plug coil stress (~3–3.9× over the design bore), the plug regime being 166–830× beyond demonstrated devices, helium-3 supply at ~400× below demand per unit, and availability of 0.86–0.995 all apply to a fixed machine exactly as stated. Fixing the site simplifies siting and shielding; it does not change plasma physics.

Any external reference to Aegis should follow this boundary: fixed defense installations, resilient sovereign power, no naval claim. The engineering case, the shielding budget, and the redundancy architecture are all written for a fixed emplacement.
A boundary that clarifies the engineering

Drawing the scope at fixed installations lets every downstream assumption be concrete: a surveyed foundation rated for the machine's mass, a shielding budget for the 5.44% neutron fraction, defined standoff distances, and space for separated redundant units. A moving platform would force all of these to be renegotiated with each deployment. The fixed-installation scope is therefore not a limitation on the ambition but a precondition for the survivability and redundancy the mission requires.

title: How the Burner Works: A Primer
lede: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a D-3He tandem-mirror generator that converts charged-particle energy directly to electricity, with a small neutron fraction and severe open gates.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) is a D–T spherical tokamak. The burner is a different machine: a D–3He tandem mirror. Deuterium fuses with helium-3, a reaction whose primary products are charged particles rather than neutrons, which is why the design targets direct energy conversion — capturing the kinetic energy of charged products as electricity instead of boiling water.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Burner energy path" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">D-3He plasma</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">tandem mirror</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Charged products</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">5.44% neutron frac</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Direct conversion</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">charge to current</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Base load</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fixed installation</text></svg>

The tandem mirror confines plasma between high-field plugs. The studied design point uses a 26.49 T plug field and a 17 T throat field. The neutron fraction is 5.44% — small compared with a D–T machine, but not zero, so shielding and activation still matter.
Conversion: direct energy conversion of charged products
Why the primer ends with gates

The same design point that produces this energy path also produces the four open gates. The plug coil is overstressed ~3–3.9× at the design bore; the plug regime is 166–830× beyond any device operated to date; helium-3 demand exceeds domestic supply by ~400× per commercial unit; and availability sits at 0.86–0.995. A primer that omitted these would misrepresent the machine. The burner is a promising study with real, named obstacles.
Why this machine, despite the gates

The reasons to study a D–<sup>3</sup>He tandem mirror for defense power are the small neutron fraction, direct energy conversion, and a fuel that can in principle be bred sovereignly. Those merits are why the gates are worth the effort rather than reasons to abandon the concept. A primer's job is to hold both in view: a machine with genuine advantages for fixed installations and with four quantified obstacles that no honest description omits.

title: Direct Energy Conversion for Bases
lede: Direct energy conversion captures charged-particle energy as electricity without a steam cycle, which is attractive for a compact, low-signature installation.
body: Most thermal power plants boil water, spin a turbine, and turn a generator. A D–3He burner produces most of its energy as fast charged particles, so the design targets direct energy conversion (DEC): decelerating those particles against an electric field and collecting the current directly. In principle this removes large rotating machinery and much of the cooling plant.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="DEC vs thermal" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Charged products</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">kinetic energy</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Decelerator</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">electric field</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Collector</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">direct current</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Conditioned output</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">to microgrid</text></svg>
Why it suits a fixed installation
Fewer large rotating parts can mean a smaller acoustic and vibration signature.
Less of the plant is a steam loop, simplifying some hardening and siting choices.
Direct collection can respond quickly, which helps a mission-critical microgrid.

None of these advantages is free, and none removes the gates. DEC still sees the 5.44% neutron fraction, so shielding and activation management remain. The plant is still built around a 26.49 T plug that is overstressed ~3–3.9× at the design bore, and it still needs helium-3 that domestic supply cannot furnish at ~400× below demand per unit.

DEC is one of the strongest reasons to study D–<sup>3</sup>He for fixed defense power, but it is an efficiency and signature argument layered on top of unresolved confinement and fuel problems. We present it as a design merit, not as a solved subsystem.
An efficiency argument, not a physics shortcut

Direct energy conversion changes how energy is collected, not whether the plasma performs. It can raise plant efficiency and lower signature, which matter greatly for a fixed installation, but it sits downstream of confinement. If the plug and regime gates are not closed, there is no charged-particle stream to convert. DEC is presented as a strong design merit layered on physics that must still be demonstrated.

title: The Fuel Convoy Problem
lede: Fixed sites that run on delivered liquid fuel depend on a logistics tail that is vulnerable, and that dependency is measured in risk to people, not only in litres.
body: A base or fixed forward site running on delivered fuel depends on a continuous logistics tail: tankers, roads, storage, and the people who move and guard them. That tail is exposed. Historically, a large share of casualties in sustained operations have been tied to protecting and moving fuel and water. The dependency is therefore best described in cost in lives, not in any monetary figure — and Kronos states it that way deliberately.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Fuel logistics tail" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Source depot</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">supply</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Convoy</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">exposed transit</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Forward storage</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fixed target</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Generators</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">continuous demand</text></svg>
How on-site generation changes the picture

A generator that runs for long intervals on a compact fuel charge shortens the tail: fewer convoys, less forward fuel storage, less of the mission spent guarding logistics. That is the central resilience argument for on-site fusion at fixed installations.
Fewer resupply movements reduce exposure of transport personnel.
Smaller forward fuel inventories present a smaller fixed target.
Less of the force is committed to protecting the logistics tail.

Fusion does not eliminate a supply chain — it changes what is supplied. The burner needs helium-3, and domestic supply is ~400× short of a single commercial unit's demand. Trading a diesel convoy for a helium-3 supply problem is only a win if that fuel can be bred (breeder) or sourced (lunar). Until then, the convoy argument is a design goal, not a delivered capability.

A fuel-dependent installation hands an adversary a repeatable, low-cost point of leverage: interdicting a route imposes a large operational penalty for a small effort. On-site generation inverts that asymmetry by removing the recurring target. The value is strategic as much as tactical — it changes what an adversary can hold at risk without ever reaching the installation itself.

title: The Cost in Lives of Fuel Logistics
lede: The dependency on delivered fuel is framed in human risk, not currency, because the people moving and guarding fuel bear the exposure.
body: Kronos does not attach monetary figures to the fuel logistics burden. The relevant cost is human: transport crews, escorts, and route-clearance personnel are exposed every time fuel moves. Framing the problem in lives keeps the argument honest and keeps it out of the economics we exclude from all public material.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Exposure layers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Route clearance</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Escort force</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Convoy crews</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Forward fuel node</text></svg>

Exposure concentrates on repetitive, predictable movements. A fixed site with a large continuous fuel demand generates frequent convoys over known routes, and predictability is itself a vulnerability. Reducing the number of movements reduces the number of times personnel are placed at risk.
Frequency of movement drives cumulative exposure.
Predictable routes and schedules compound the risk.
Forward fuel storage is a fixed, locatable point of vulnerability.
What fusion would and would not change

A long-interval on-site generator reduces movement frequency, and that is a genuine reduction in exposure. It does not remove all logistics: the machine still needs helium-3, spares, and maintenance access. And it is not fieldable today — the burner's plug, regime, fuel, and availability gates are unresolved. The life-safety argument motivates the work; it does not pre-empt the physics.
Why the framing is kept human

Attaching currency to this problem would both violate the economics exclusion and understate it: the burden that matters is exposure of people. Keeping the framing in lives forces the design conversation to focus on reducing movements and forward storage rather than on any monetary accounting, which is the correct engineering objective for a resilience programme.

title: Reducing the Logistics Tail
lede: On-site generation shortens the chain of people and vehicles a fixed installation depends on, subject to a different, unresolved fuel supply for fusion.
body: The logistics tail is everything upstream of a base's power that must keep flowing for the lights to stay on: fuel sources, transport, escorts, storage, and maintenance. For a fuel-fed installation the tail is long and continuous. Shortening it is a primary aim of on-site sovereign power.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Tail before vs after" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Long tail</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">frequent convoys</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">On-site gen</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">long fuel interval</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Short tail</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fewer movements</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Residual</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">spares + He-3</text></svg>
Movement frequency drops when a fuel charge lasts a long interval.
Forward fuel storage shrinks, reducing a fixed vulnerability.
Personnel committed to escorting fuel can be reassigned.

Fusion substitutes one supply problem for another. The burner needs helium-3, and per-unit demand is ~400× domestic supply, so the fusion tail runs to a fuel that does not yet exist at terrestrial scale. It also needs cryogens, spares, and skilled maintenance. The honest claim is that the tail changes shape — from bulk liquid fuel to a small mass of scarce isotope plus a maintenance chain — not that it vanishes.

This is why the breeder matters to the defense story: it breeds helium-3 and tritium domestically, and lunar helium-3 is the longer-term source. The logistics case for the burner is contingent on that fuel pathway being real.
A change of shape, stated precisely

The honest formulation is a shift from a large, frequent, bulk-fuel tail to a small, infrequent, high-assurance isotope-plus-maintenance tail. That is a real improvement in exposure and in independence duration, and it is conditional on the sovereign helium-3 pathway existing. Naming both halves keeps the logistics claim credible rather than absolute.

title: Energy Independence for Bases
lede: Energy independence means a fixed installation can generate what it needs without a grid tie or a fuel convoy, within the limits the availability gate imposes.
body: For a defense installation, energy independence is the ability to meet mission power demand from on-site generation, indefinitely, without relying on a commercial utility or a continuous fuel delivery. It is the combination of a long-interval generator, an islanded microgrid, and enough redundancy to survive single failures.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Independence stack" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Sovereign fuel</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">On-site generation</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Islanded microgrid</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Redundant trains</text></svg>

A D–<sup>3</sup>He burner running on a compact fuel charge is, in principle, a strong contributor to independence: it decouples the base from grid outages and from fuel-route interdiction. Direct energy conversion and a small 5.44% neutron fraction make it comparatively compact for its output.

Independence is not the same as uninterrupted. The burner's studied availability is 0.86–0.995, against a hyperscale Tier III reference of 0.99982 — 30–100× more downtime. A single unit cannot, on those figures, be the sole source for a continuous mission. Independence at the installation level therefore requires redundancy: multiple units, storage, and a backup path.
One unit reduces external dependency but is not a sole source.
Redundant units plus storage close the availability gap at the system level.
The fuel must be sovereign (bred or lunar) for independence to be genuine.
Energy independence is achievable as a system property, not from a single machine, and not before the burner's gates are resolved.

No single generator confers independence; the combination of a long-interval source, an islandable microgrid, storage, and redundancy does. Because a burner sits at 0.86–0.995 availability, independence at the installation level is a property of the whole architecture designed to the honest number, with sovereign fuel as the upstream precondition.

title: Islanded Microgrid Architecture
lede: An islanded microgrid lets a base generate, distribute, and control its own power with no reliance on a commercial grid, using the fusion unit as one dispatchable source.
body: An islanded microgrid is a self-contained electrical system that generates and distributes power within an installation's boundary, able to run disconnected from any commercial grid. For a defense site, islanding is the default posture: the base is designed to operate as though the outside grid does not exist.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Microgrid elements" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion unit</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">dispatchable</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Storage</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">ride-through</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Controller</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">dispatch + protect</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Mission loads</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">prioritised</text></svg>
Generation: the fusion unit as a base-load source, plus backup generation.
Storage: batteries or equivalent to smooth transients and bridge trips.
Controls: a microgrid controller that dispatches sources and sheds non-critical load.
Protection: fault isolation so one failure does not black out the mission loads.
Why the fusion unit is not the whole grid

Because burner availability is 0.86–0.995 versus Tier III's 0.99982, the microgrid must be designed so the mission survives a unit trip. Storage bridges short outages; redundant generation covers longer ones; load-shedding protects the highest-priority loads. The fusion unit is the anchor source, not the entire architecture.

This architecture is standard microgrid engineering applied to a novel source. It is the layer that turns an imperfect generator into resilient installation power — and it is why sovereign power is a system claim, not a single-machine claim.

A defense microgrid is designed to run islanded as its normal state and to treat any external connection as optional. This inverts the civilian assumption that the grid is primary and on-site generation is backup. The fusion unit anchors the islanded base load, while storage, controls, and redundancy give the island the continuity a single machine cannot.

title: Black-Start Capability
lede: Black-start is the ability to bring an installation's power up from a fully de-energised state without external support; a fusion microgrid must plan for it explicitly.
body: Black-start is restarting a power system from complete shutdown with no outside energy. For a defense installation that has been isolated or has suffered a total outage, black-start is the difference between hours and days to restore the mission.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Black-start sequence" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Cold start source</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">battery / small gen</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Auxiliaries</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">cryo + controls</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion unit</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">bring to power</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Mission loads</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">re-energise</text></svg>
The challenge for a fusion unit

A tandem-mirror burner is not self-starting. It needs auxiliary power to energise magnets, run cryogenics for its high-field coils, and drive plasma heating before it can produce net output. That means black-start depends on a smaller, independent starting source — storage or a small backup generator — sized to bring the fusion plant's auxiliaries up first.
A cold-start source (storage or small generator) energises first.
Cryogenic and control auxiliaries come up before the plasma.
The fusion unit is then brought to power and picks up mission loads.

Startup time for a high-field fusion machine is not short, and the burner is a design study, not built hardware. Black-start planning must therefore assume the fusion unit is the last source restored, with storage and backup generation carrying the mission during the interval. This reinforces the redundancy theme: resilient sovereign power is a layered system in which fusion is the anchor, not the first responder.

Black-start is only a capability if it is proceduralised and tested: the cold-start source sized correctly, the auxiliary-energisation sequence validated, and the fusion unit's long start-up time accounted for. An untested black-start plan is not resilience. The design treats black-start as a rehearsed procedure with the fusion unit as the last, not the first, source restored.

title: Continuity of Operations
lede: Continuity of operations is the ability to keep mission power flowing through faults, attacks, and maintenance, achieved by layering the fusion unit with storage and redundancy.
body: Continuity of operations for installation power means the mission never loses the electricity it depends on, across the full range of disruptions: grid loss, fuel interdiction, equipment faults, planned maintenance, and attack. No single machine delivers continuity; it is a property of the whole power architecture.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Continuity layers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Redundant generation</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Energy storage</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Fusion anchor unit</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Protected mission loads</text></svg>
Fuel interdiction — addressed by long-interval on-site fuel.
Equipment fault or trip — addressed by redundancy and storage.
Planned maintenance — addressed by N+1 units.

A burner with 0.86–0.995 availability will trip and will need maintenance windows. Continuity requires that these expected outages are covered: storage bridges seconds-to-minutes, a second unit or backup generation covers hours-to-days. Designing to the honest availability figure — rather than an aspirational one — is what makes continuity real.

Continuity of operations is the outcome that resilient sovereign power aims to deliver, and it is achievable at the installation level with a layered architecture even though the fusion unit itself is not, on its own, continuous.
Designing to expected, not ideal, behaviour

Continuity is achieved by planning for the outages that will happen — trips, faults, and maintenance implied by 0.86–0.995 availability — and covering each with the right layer: storage for seconds to minutes, redundant units for hours to days. Continuity built on an optimistic availability number is fragile; continuity built on the honest one is real.

title: The Availability Gate Explained
lede: Studied burner availability of 0.86-0.995 is 30-100x more downtime than a hyperscale Tier III reference of 0.99982, so a single unit cannot be a sole source today.
body: Availability is the fraction of time a source is producing usable power. The burner's studied availability is 0.86 to 0.995. The reference for a hyperscale, mission-critical facility — Tier III — is 0.99982. The gap is large: measured in downtime, the burner is roughly 30 to 100 times further from continuous than Tier III.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 148" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Availability comparison" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner (low)</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="327" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">0.860</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner (high)</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="378" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">0.995</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Tier III</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">0.99982</text></svg>
What the gap means in downtime

Tier III 0.99982 corresponds to well under an hour of downtime per year. Burner availability of 0.995 corresponds to on the order of a day-and-a-half per year, and 0.86 to weeks per year. For a continuous mission, that is the difference between negligible and mission-affecting — unless the system is designed to cover it.
A single burner unit is not a sole Tier-III-class source today.
Redundancy (N+1 units, storage, backup generation) closes the gap at the system level.
Availability is expected to improve from FOAK to NOAK to BOAK, but that is a projection, not a result.

This gate is a physics-and-engineering fact about a machine that is not yet built. It is not translated into any cost or price figure. Stating it up front is what lets the redundancy architecture be designed honestly rather than around an optimistic number.
Why we lead with this number

Availability is the single figure that most often gets rounded up in resilient-power claims. Kronos states it at full candor because the entire redundancy architecture depends on it being honest. A design sized to 0.99982 that the machine cannot meet would fail in the field; a design sized to 0.86–0.995 with redundancy meets the mission. The gate is a design input, never translated into any price or cost.

title: Availability Math and the Downtime Budget
lede: Turning availability figures into an annual downtime budget shows exactly how much redundancy a mission-critical installation must carry.
body: Availability A relates to annual downtime by (1 − A) × 8,766 hours. Working the burner and Tier III numbers gives a concrete downtime budget that drives the redundancy design.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 148" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Annual downtime (relative)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Tier III 0.99982</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="8" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~1.6 h/yr</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner 0.995</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="106" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~44 h/yr</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner 0.86</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~1,227 h/yr</text></svg>
Tier III 0.99982 → about 1.6 hours of downtime per year.
Burner 0.86 → about 1,227 hours per year (~51 days).

If a mission needs Tier-III-class continuity from sources that individually deliver 0.86–0.995, the system must carry parallel capacity and fast-switching storage so that one unit's downtime is invisible to the load. Two independent units, each at 0.995, combined so either can carry the load, give a combined unavailability far below a single unit — approaching the Tier III target as units and storage are added.

The point of the math is not to claim the burner reaches Tier III. It is to size the redundancy honestly. The downtime budget is the design input; the redundancy architecture is the response. No monetary values enter this calculation — it is purely time and reliability.

The downtime budget is what converts an abstract availability figure into concrete redundancy: how many parallel units, how much storage, and how fast a spare must pick up load. Two independent units near 0.995 combine to an unavailability far below either alone, approaching the Tier III target as units are added. The math is purely reliability and time, with no economic content.

title: Redundancy and N+1
lede: Because a single burner unit is not continuous, resilient installation power depends on N+1 (or greater) redundancy so any one failure is covered.
body: N+1 redundancy means an installation carries at least one more generating unit than it needs to meet peak demand, so any single unit can fail or be maintained without losing the mission. For higher assurance, N+2 or 2N architectures carry more margin still.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="N+1 layout" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Unit 1</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">carrying load</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Unit 2</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">carrying load</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Unit +1</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">spare / rotating</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Storage</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">bridge on trip</text></svg>

With availability at 0.86–0.995, a single burner will be down for a meaningful fraction of the year. Redundancy converts many imperfect units into a highly available system: when units fail independently, the probability that all redundant units are down at once falls sharply as units are added.
N+1: mission survives any single unit outage.
N+2 / 2N: mission survives concurrent outages, including maintenance during a fault.
Storage covers the switching interval between a trip and a spare picking up load.
The honest cost is hardware, not currency

Redundancy is paid in equipment, space, and fuel, which we describe qualitatively only. What matters for the physics story is that redundancy is mandatory, not optional, given the availability gate. A resilient sovereign installation is a small fleet of units plus storage, engineered so the whole is far more available than any part.
Independence of failures is the assumption to protect

Redundancy only multiplies availability if failures are independent, so the architecture separates units physically, powers them from independent auxiliaries, and avoids shared single points such as one control path or one cooling source. A common-cause failure that takes several units at once would defeat the redundancy, so eliminating shared dependencies is as important as adding units.

title: Reliability Growth: FOAK to NOAK
lede: Availability is expected to improve across the first-of-a-kind, next-of-a-kind, and best-of-a-kind builds, but that improvement is a projection until hardware demonstrates it.
body: Why first units are least reliable

First-of-a-kind (FOAK) machines are where unknown failure modes surface. As designs mature through next-of-a-kind (NOAK) and best-of-a-kind (BOAK) builds, components are refined, maintenance is understood, and availability typically climbs. This reliability growth is a well-observed pattern in complex systems.

Applying it honestly to the burner

The burner has not been built, so its FOAK availability is not measured. The 0.86–0.995 range spans this expected growth. It would be dishonest to quote the top of the range as a delivered figure, and dishonest to ignore that growth is expected. Both statements are true: early units will be less available, and the design intent is to improve.
The breeder (Hyperion) reaches FOAK first tritium ~2030, demonstrating the harder fuel-cycle physics.
The burner's plug, regime, and fuel gates must be resolved before a burner FOAK exists.
Availability growth is validated by operating hardware, not by extrapolation.

Reliability growth is a reason for optimism about the mature machine and a reason for caution about the first one. Resilient sovereign power is designed for the availability we can defend today, with growth treated as upside to be proven.

Reliability growth is a well-attested pattern, but treating projected NOAK or BOAK availability as if it were a delivered figure would be dishonest. The design baseline is what the current machine can defend; growth is upside to be proven in hardware. This keeps the resilient-power case anchored to demonstrated capability while acknowledging the expected trajectory.

title: Gate: Plug Coil Overstressed 3-3.9x
lede: At the design bore, the burner's high-field plug coil is overstressed by roughly 3 to 3.9 times, making it infeasible as specified without a materials or geometry change.
body: The tandem mirror needs a very high plug field — 26.49 T — produced by a compact plug coil. At the studied bore, the mechanical stress in that coil exceeds what the conductor and structure can bear by a factor of roughly 3 to 3.9. As specified, the plug coil is infeasible: it would fail structurally.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 148" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Plug coil stress vs limit" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Structural limit</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="106" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">1.0x (allowable)</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Design bore (low)</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="323" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~3.0x</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Design bore (high)</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~3.9x</text></svg>
Why the field is so demanding

High plug fields are what make the tandem-mirror confinement work at all; the physics wants a large field, and a large field in a small bore concentrates enormous magnetic pressure in the coil structure. The stress scales steeply, so modest field increases become severe structural problems.
Higher-strength or differently reinforced conductor and structure.
Revised coil geometry and bore that trade field profile against stress.
Materials advances validated by 14 MeV neutron irradiation testing from the breeder.

This is the first and most concrete gate: a specific, quantified structural overstress. It is stated as a physics-and-engineering fact. Until a coil design carries 26.49 T within allowable stress, the burner is not buildable as specified, and no downstream capability claim can stand ahead of it.
The most concrete of the four gates

Unlike a diffuse uncertainty, the plug-coil overstress is a specific, quantified structural result: roughly 3 to 3.9 times the allowable stress at the design bore. It is falsifiable and it is a hard stop — a coil cannot carry a load it fails under. Every downstream capability claim for the burner is subordinate to a coil design that carries 26.49 T within allowable stress.

title: Gate: Plug Regime 166-830x Beyond Devices
lede: The burner's plug operates in a plasma regime 166 to 830 times beyond any device ever run, so its behaviour cannot be post-dicted from existing data today.
body: Confidence in a plasma design comes from post-diction: reproducing the behaviour of machines that have actually run. The burner's plug regime sits 166 to 830 times beyond the parameter space of any device operated to date. There is no experimental anchor at those conditions, so the plug's behaviour cannot be validated against data today.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 148" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Distance from demonstrated regime" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Demonstrated devices</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="8" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">1x</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner plug (low)</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="76" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">166x</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Burner plug (high)</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">830x</text></svg>

Plasma behaviour is nonlinear; instabilities and transport can change character across such a gap. Extrapolating 100–800× beyond any operating point is not a small correction — it is a leap into unmeasured physics. A design that works on paper at those conditions has not been shown to work in a machine, because no machine has been there.
Intermediate experiments that step the regime forward and anchor the models.
Validated simulation benchmarked against those experiments, not against nothing.
Honest reporting of remaining extrapolation risk at each step.

This gate is why Kronos calls the burner a design-and-simulation study. The plug regime is currently un-post-dictable, and no amount of internal simulation substitutes for a machine at the relevant conditions. Resilient sovereign power from the burner is contingent on this gate being closed experimentally.
No substitute for a machine at the conditions

Internal simulation, however careful, cannot validate physics at 166–830 times beyond any operating point, because there is no data at those conditions to check it against. Closing this gate requires intermediate experiments that step the regime forward and anchor the models. Until then, burner performance in the plug is a projection, and Kronos labels it as one.

title: Gate: Helium-3 Demand ~400x Supply
lede: A single commercial burner unit would demand roughly 400 times the domestic helium-3 supply, so the machine is gated on a fuel that does not exist at terrestrial scale.
body: The burner fuses deuterium with helium-3. Helium-3 is extraordinarily scarce on Earth. A single commercial burner unit would require on the order of 400 times the entire domestic helium-3 supply per year. The fuel simply does not exist at the scale one commercial machine needs, let alone a fleet.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 114" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="He-3: demand vs domestic supply" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Domestic supply</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="8" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">1x</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">One commercial unit</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">~400x</text></svg>
Why this is the deepest gate

Plug stress and regime are engineering and physics problems on the machine. The fuel gate is upstream of the machine entirely: even a perfect burner cannot run without helium-3. Terrestrial helium-3 comes largely from tritium decay in limited stockpiles — nowhere near fleet demand.
The two pathways that make the burner conceivable
Breeder-bred: the breeder (Hyperion) produces a helium-3 stream (~1.97 kg/yr class) and tritium (~4 kg/yr class), tritium decaying to helium-3 — a domestic, sovereign source.
Lunar helium-3: the regolith holds helium-3 implanted by the solar wind, a longer-term extraterrestrial source.

This gate is precisely why the breeder and lunar helium-3 are central to the defense story rather than side notes. Without a sovereign helium-3 pathway, the burner's resilient-power promise is unbacked. With one, the fuel argument becomes a supply-chain to build rather than a physical impossibility.
The gate upstream of the machine

Plug stress and regime are problems on the machine; the fuel gate is upstream of it entirely. Even a flawless burner cannot run without helium-3, and terrestrial supply is roughly 400 times short of a single commercial unit's annual demand. This is why the breeder's bred helium-3 and, at fleet scale, lunar helium-3 are load-bearing parts of the strategy rather than footnotes.

title: Why Breeder-Bred and Lunar Helium-3 Matter
lede: The burner's fuel gate is only answerable by a sovereign helium-3 pathway: breeder-bred isotopes now and lunar helium-3 later.
body: The fuel gate demands a source

Because a commercial burner needs ~400× domestic helium-3 supply, the machine is only credible if a new, sovereign helium-3 source exists. Two pathways are studied, and together they connect the breeder, the Moon, and the burner into one strategy.
