Fuel: multiple sovereign helium-3 sources (breeder-bred, later lunar) plus buffer inventory.
Spares: on-site stock and modular design for fast swap-out.
Materials: qualified domestic suppliers for magnets, cryogenics, structures.
Skills: trained operators and maintainers, not a single-point human dependency.

The dominant upstream vulnerability today is the helium-3 fuel itself: at ~400× domestic supply per unit, the supply chain for the burner's fuel does not yet exist at scale. Supply-chain resilience for burner power is therefore partly a future-build task — standing up the breeder-bred and lunar pathways — not only a matter of buffering an existing supply.

Resilient sovereign power requires resilient supply. On-site fusion trades a large, exposed fuel convoy for a smaller, higher-assurance supply chain that must itself be engineered for resilience and, in the case of the fuel, largely built from scratch.

On-site fusion removes the fuel convoy but introduces helium-3 supply, spares, materials, and skills as upstream dependencies. The dominant one today is the fuel itself: at ~400× demand per unit, that supply chain does not yet exist at scale. Resilience here is partly a future-build task — standing up the breeder-bred and lunar pathways — not only buffering an existing supply.

title: Resilience Metrics and Definitions
lede: Resilience is measurable: availability, reliability, ride-through, restoration time, and independence duration each capture part of it.
body: Resilience is often used loosely; here it is broken into measurable properties. Each captures a distinct aspect of how well installation power survives disruption, and each can be designed to and reported honestly.
Availability: fraction of time producing usable power (burner 0.86–0.995).
Reliability: probability of running without failure over a mission interval.
Ride-through: how long the system carries load through a source loss.
Restoration time: how fast full power returns after an outage (MTTR + black-start).
Independence duration: how long the base runs with no external supply.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 148" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Resilience dimensions (illustrative)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Availability</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="342" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">per unit</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Ride-through</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="228" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">storage-set</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Independence</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="304" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">fuel-set</text></svg>

No single number captures resilience. A unit can have high independence duration (long fuel interval) but modest availability (trips and maintenance). The system-level goal is to combine sources so that every metric meets the mission requirement, not just one. Reporting all of them prevents a favourable number from masking a weak one.

Kronos reports the availability figure that the physics and engineering support (0.86–0.995), against the Tier III reference (0.99982), rather than an aspirational single value. The other metrics are set largely by the storage and redundancy design, which is where much of the resilience is actually engineered.

A unit can have long independence duration but modest availability, so reporting one favourable metric can mask a weak one. The system goal is that every dimension — availability, reliability, ride-through, restoration time, independence duration — meets the mission requirement. Kronos reports the availability the physics supports (0.86–0.995) against the Tier III reference, not an aspirational single value.

title: Comparison to Diesel Generation
lede: Compared with diesel gensets, a fusion installation trades a continuous fuel convoy and large signature for a hard fuel gate and imperfect availability.
body: Diesel and gas gensets are the incumbent for fixed installation power. Comparing them with a fusion installation is instructive — kept strictly qualitative, with no cost or price figures on either side.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 182" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Qualitative comparison (higher = better)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: low signature</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="342" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">strong</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: fuel convoy</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="323" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">much reduced</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: availability</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="152" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">gated</text><text x="10" y="150" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: readiness</text><rect x="220" y="136" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="136" width="57" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="150" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">design stage</text></svg>
Signature: no combustion exhaust plume; lower acoustic signature with direct conversion.
Logistics tail: a long fuel interval versus continuous diesel resupply.
Emissions: no combustion emissions during operation.
Where diesel is still ahead today
Readiness: diesel is proven and fielded; the burner is a design study.
Availability: mature gensets are highly available; the burner is 0.86–0.995.
Fuel supply: diesel supply exists; helium-3 is ~400× short of demand per unit.

The honest picture is a technology with clear advantages in signature and logistics that is not yet a substitute for diesel on readiness, availability, or fuel supply. In any near-term architecture, fusion complements — and reduces reliance on — diesel rather than replacing it outright. Diesel remains part of the backup and black-start layer.

The honest picture is a technology with clear signature and logistics advantages that is not yet a substitute for diesel on readiness, availability, or fuel supply. In any near-term architecture, fusion reduces reliance on diesel rather than replacing it; diesel remains part of the backup and black-start layer. The comparison is kept strictly qualitative on both sides.

title: Comparison to Small Modular Reactors
lede: Fission microreactors and fusion installations both offer long-interval on-site power; they differ in fuel, waste, signature, and readiness.
body: Small modular reactors (SMRs) and microreactors are the other candidate for long-interval, low-convoy installation power. A fair comparison with a fusion burner is qualitative and acknowledges that fission microreactors are far closer to fielding today.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 182" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Qualitative differences" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><text x="10" y="48" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: readiness</text><rect x="220" y="34" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="34" width="76" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="48" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">design stage</text><text x="10" y="82" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fission micro: readiness</text><rect x="220" y="68" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="68" width="266" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">nearer term</text><text x="10" y="116" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: long-lived waste</text><rect x="220" y="102" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="102" width="342" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="116" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">much less</text><text x="10" y="150" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion: fuel availability</text><rect x="220" y="136" width="380" height="18" rx="4" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.5"/><rect x="220" y="136" width="76" height="18" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="608" y="150" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11.5" font-weight="600">He-3 gated</text></svg>
Waste: D–<sup>3</sup>He produces far less long-lived waste; only the 5.44% neutron fraction activates structures.
Fuel: fission fuel supply is established; helium-3 is ~400× short of demand per unit.
Signature: direct conversion offers a low acoustic signature; both have thermal signatures.
Readiness: fission microreactors are nearer to fielding; the burner is a design study with open gates.

Fusion's long-term advantages — minimal long-lived waste and, potentially, a sovereign bred fuel — are real, but fission microreactors lead decisively on near-term readiness and on fuel availability. The burner is not presented as a competitor to fielded fission today; it is a longer-horizon option whose distinctive merits depend on closing its plug, regime, fuel, and availability gates.

For an installation planner, the two are not mutually exclusive: near-term resilience may come from one technology while the fusion pathway matures. This comparison is deliberately free of economics on either side.

Fission microreactors lead decisively on near-term readiness and fuel availability, while the burner's distinctive merits — minimal long-lived waste and a potentially sovereign bred fuel — depend on closing its gates. For a planner the two are not mutually exclusive: near-term resilience may come from one technology while the fusion pathway matures. No economics enters this comparison.

title: Thermal Management and Waste Heat
lede: Every power plant rejects waste heat; managing it well serves efficiency, signature, and siting all at once.
body: No generator converts all its energy to electricity; the remainder is waste heat that must be rejected. Even with direct energy conversion, the burner rejects heat from its magnets, cryogenics, and conversion losses. Managing that heat is a core plant engineering task.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Heat management" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Waste heat</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">from plant</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Heat rejection</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">radiators / towers</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Optional reuse</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">space / process</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Reduced plume</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">managed</text></svg>
Efficiency: less rejected heat per unit output improves overall performance.
Signature: the heat rejection plume is the dominant residual thermal signature.
Siting: cooling infrastructure needs space, water or air, and placement.
Reuse: waste heat can serve space or process heating, improving total utilisation.

The burner's high-field magnets require cryogenic cooling, which itself consumes power and rejects heat at the warm end. Thermal management therefore spans both the very cold (magnet cryogenics) and the warm (heat rejection) ends of the plant. Good design minimises the parasitic load and the external signature together.

Thermal management is mature engineering applied to a novel machine. It does not affect the plasma gates, but it strongly affects signature and siting — two of the reasons the burner is attractive for defense installations in the first place — so it is treated as a first-order design task.

The burner spans the very cold, from cryogenic magnets, and the warm, at heat rejection, so thermal management addresses both a parasitic cryogenic load and an external heat plume. Minimising the parasitic draw and the thermal signature are the same design task. Waste-heat reuse for space or process heat improves total utilisation while reducing what must be rejected.

title: Environmental Siting Considerations
lede: A fusion installation must be sited responsibly for water, land, activation, and local impact, consistent with a fixed emplacement's obligations.
body: Beyond hardening and survivability, a fixed installation carries environmental obligations: water for cooling, land footprint, management of activated materials from the 5.44% neutron fraction, and local environmental impact. Responsible siting addresses all of these at the design stage.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Siting factors" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Local impact</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Water / cooling</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Activation mgmt</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Machine footprint</text></svg>
Water and cooling availability, or air-cooling where water is scarce.
Management and eventual disposition of activated structural materials.
Land footprint for the machine, shielding, storage, and redundant units.
Local environmental and community impact for a permanent emplacement.

Relative to combustion generation, the burner has no operational combustion emissions, and relative to fission its long-lived waste is far smaller — only structures activated by the small neutron fraction require management. These are genuine environmental advantages. They do not remove the obligation to site responsibly, particularly regarding water, land, and activated-material handling.

Environmental siting is a design-stage discipline for a fixed installation. It is presented honestly: fusion improves the operational environmental profile substantially but still requires careful, responsible siting like any major power installation.
A favourable profile that still needs care

Relative to combustion the burner has no operational emissions, and relative to fission its long-lived waste is far smaller, with only activated structures to manage. These are genuine advantages that do not remove the obligation to site responsibly for water, land, and activated-material handling. Environmental siting is a design-stage discipline like it is for any major installation.

title: Decommissioning and Lifecycle
lede: A fixed installation must be planned for its whole life, including eventual decommissioning of activated structures and management of residual materials.
body: Resilient power is a long-term commitment, and a responsible design accounts for the full lifecycle: construction, operation, maintenance, upgrades, and eventual decommissioning. For a fusion installation this includes managing structures activated by the 5.44% neutron fraction at end of life.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Lifecycle" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Construct</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">emplace</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Operate</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">maintain + upgrade</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Decommission</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">manage activation</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Site release</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">restore</text></svg>
Managing structural materials activated over the machine's life.
Recovering and accounting for residual helium-3 and tritium inventory.
Dismantling magnets, cryogenics, and shielding safely.

Because D–<sup>3</sup>He carries only a small neutron fraction, the volume of activated material at decommissioning is far smaller than for a D–T fusion plant or a fission reactor, and there is no long-lived spent-fuel stream. Material choices during design (low-activation alloys, informed by 14 MeV neutron testing from the breeder) can reduce it further.

Lifecycle planning is a mark of a serious, honest design. It is included here to show that resilient sovereign power is scoped as a full-life capability — not only how it starts, but how it is maintained and responsibly retired — even while the machine itself remains at the design-and-simulation stage.
Planned retirement is a mark of seriousness

Because D–<sup>3</sup>He carries only a small neutron fraction, the volume of activated material at end of life is far smaller than for a D–T plant or a fission reactor, with no long-lived spent-fuel stream. Low-activation material choices, informed by 14 MeV neutron testing from the breeder, reduce it further. Scoping the full life — not only how power starts but how it is responsibly retired — is part of an honest design.

title: Simulation vs Hardware: An Honest Line
lede: The burner's resilient-power case rests on design and simulation; the line between what is simulated and what is demonstrated is drawn explicitly.
body: Everything on these pages about the burner is design and simulation. No burner has been built. The breeder (Hyperion) begins construction Q2 2027 and targets FOAK first tritium ~2030; the burner is a later, harder machine. Confusing simulation with demonstration would be the most damaging thing a resilient-power claim could do.

What simulation can and cannot establish
Can: explore design points, size subsystems, identify and quantify gates.
Can: bound performance and expose infeasibilities (e.g., plug stress 3–3.9×).
Cannot: validate physics in a regime 166–830× beyond any device.
Cannot: substitute for measured availability, MTTR, or hardware behaviour.

Kronos states which numbers are design points (Q_sci 3.424, 88.7 MW and the breeder parameters; 26.49 T plug, 5.44% neutron fraction for the burner) and which are open gates (plug stress, plug regime, helium-3 supply, availability). The frozen design figures are used exactly; the gates are stated at full candor. This is how a design-stage claim earns trust.

The honest line is simple: the burner is a credible design with named, quantified obstacles, evaluated in simulation, awaiting the experiments and hardware that alone can promote simulation to demonstration.

Simulation can explore design points, size subsystems, and expose infeasibilities such as the 3–3.9× plug overstress, but it cannot validate physics 166–830× beyond any device or substitute for measured availability and repair times. Only intermediate experiments and, ultimately, hardware promote a simulation result to a demonstrated one. Kronos labels which numbers are design points and which are open gates.

title: Timeline and Design-Stage Status
lede: The breeder leads on a defined timeline; the burner that delivers resilient power is a later machine gated on its own physics.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) construction begins Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium targeted around 2030; next-of-a-kind (NOAK) and best-of-a-kind (BOAK) units follow. There is no hardware net-gain claim before FOAK. The burner that would provide resilient installation power is a subsequent, harder programme.

It proves the harder D–T fuel-cycle physics in hardware.
It breeds the helium-3 and tritium the burner needs (fuel gate).

The burner's resilient-power promise is contingent on closing its plug-stress (3–3.9×), plug-regime (166–830×), fuel-supply (~400×), and availability (0.86–0.995) gates. None is closed today. The burner is therefore a design-and-simulation study whose fielding lies beyond the breeder's demonstration and beyond intermediate experiments that must anchor the plug regime.

Stating the timeline honestly — breeder now, burner later, both gated — is essential. Resilient sovereign power from fusion is a direction with a credible first step (the breeder) and a demanding path beyond it, not a near-term product.

The breeder leads because it proves the harder D–T fuel-cycle physics in hardware, breeds the helium-3 and tritium the burner needs, and produces 14 MeV neutrons to qualify burner materials. The burner's resilient-power promise is contingent on closing its four gates, none closed today, so its fielding lies beyond the breeder's demonstration and beyond the intermediate experiments that must anchor the plug regime.

title: Honest Readiness Summary: Power
lede: A single-page summary of what resilient sovereign power from the burner offers, and the four physics gates that stand between the concept and hardware.
body: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), studied for fixed defense installations, offers a compelling resilient-power concept: on-site, islandable, low-signature base-load generation that shortens the fuel-convoy logistics tail and, with a sovereign fuel pathway, provides power under national control. Direct energy conversion and a small 5.44% neutron fraction make it comparatively compact and clean.

Plug regime 166–830× beyond any device — un-post-dictable today.
Helium-3 demand ~400× domestic supply per unit — fuel does not exist at scale.
Availability 0.86–0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982 — 30–100× short on downtime.

The burner is a design-and-simulation study, not fielded hardware, and not a sole-source power solution today. Its resilient-power value is real and worth pursuing, but it is delivered as a redundant system, contingent on breeder-bred and lunar helium-3, and gated on physics that the breeder programme and intermediate experiments are meant to help close.
Kronos states these gates plainly because candor is the foundation of a defense relationship. The promise is significant; the path to it is demanding and named.

Stating the four gates plainly — plug stress, plug regime, helium-3 supply, availability — is what makes a defense relationship possible. The promise of on-site, islandable, low-signature, sovereignly-fuelled power is significant and worth pursuing; the path to it is demanding and named. Kronos offers today a disciplined way of designing toward that capability, not fielded hardware.

title: Continuity During Maintenance
lede: Planned maintenance is a predictable outage that must be covered by redundancy so the mission never loses power during servicing.
body: Unlike a fault, maintenance is scheduled — which makes it fully coverable. But a high-field fusion unit needs real maintenance windows: magnets and cryogenics do not warm and cool quickly, and inspection of a machine with an activated first structure takes time. Continuity requires these windows to be invisible to the mission.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Maintenance coverage" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Unit down</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">planned window</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Redundant unit</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">carries load</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Storage</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">covers switch</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Mission</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">uninterrupted</text></svg>
N+1 units so one can be serviced while others carry the load.
Scheduling maintenance during lower-demand periods where possible.
Modular design to shorten the maintenance window (lower MTTR).
Storage to cover the transition as load moves between units.
Why it is part of the availability figure

The 0.86–0.995 availability range already folds in maintenance downtime, not only unplanned faults. Because maintenance is predictable, it is the easiest part of unavailability to cover with redundancy. A well-run installation loses no mission power to servicing, even though each unit spends real time offline for it.

Continuity during maintenance is a straightforward consequence of the redundancy the availability gate already requires. It is worth stating explicitly because it shows the gate is managed, not ignored: expected downtime is designed for, so the mission does not feel it.
The most coverable part of the gate

Because maintenance is scheduled, it is the easiest component of unavailability to cover: an N+1 architecture lets one unit be serviced while others carry the load, storage covers the transition, and modular design shortens the window. The 0.86–0.995 range already folds in maintenance, so a well-run installation loses no mission power to servicing even though each unit spends real time offline.

title: Black-Start of a Base Microgrid
lede: Restoring a whole base microgrid from cold requires a deliberate sequence in which the fusion unit is brought up last, after a smaller starting source.
body: If an installation goes fully dark — grid lost, all generation down — the base must black-start: bring its microgrid back up from nothing. For a fusion-anchored microgrid this is a sequenced operation, because the fusion unit itself needs power to start.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Microgrid black-start" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Cold start</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">battery / small gen</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Energise bus</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">controls + protection</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion aux</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">cryo + magnets</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Full power</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">mission restored</text></svg>
A black-start source (storage or a small generator) energises first.
The microgrid bus, controls, and protection come alive.
Fusion auxiliaries — cryogenics, magnet supplies, heating — are powered.
The fusion unit reaches power and assumes the base load.

Because the fusion unit cannot start itself and is not quick to bring to power, the microgrid must include an independent black-start capability sized to energise the fusion plant's auxiliaries. This is a specific, deliberate design requirement, not an assumption. The fusion unit is the anchor for steady-state power and the last element restored during a black-start.

Black-start planning ties together storage, backup generation, and controls into a tested restoration procedure. It is another expression of the layered architecture: fusion provides the enduring power, but simpler sources provide the spark that brings it back after a total loss.

Restoring a dark base is a deliberate sequence: an independent black-start source energises first, then the bus and controls, then the fusion plant's auxiliaries, and finally the machine reaches power and assumes the base load. Because the fusion unit cannot start itself and is slow to bring to power, the black-start source is a specific sized requirement, and the fusion unit is the last element restored.

title: Mission Assurance and Power
lede: Mission assurance treats power as a mission-essential function to be guaranteed end to end, aligning power design with the operations it supports.
body: Mission assurance is the discipline of guaranteeing that mission-essential functions continue under stress. Power is foundational: command, communications, sensors, and life-safety all fail without it. Treating power as a mission-essential function means designing, testing, and operating it to the same assurance standard as the mission itself.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Assurance layers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Mission function</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Assured power</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Redundant sources</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Tested procedures</text></svg>
Identifying which loads are mission-essential and their tolerance to interruption.
Designing sources and storage to meet those tolerances with margin.
Testing failure and restoration procedures, including black-start.
Continuously monitoring the health of every source and path.

The availability gate (0.86–0.995) sets how much redundancy assurance requires. The fuel gate (~400×) sets a supply dependency that assurance planning must cover with sovereign sources and buffers. The plug and regime gates keep the burner at the design stage, so mission assurance today treats fusion as a future anchor and relies on proven sources for present missions.

Mission assurance is the operational framing that ties every resilient-power page together: availability, redundancy, fuel, hardening, controls, and black-start are all in service of guaranteeing the mission-essential function of power. It keeps the engineering honest by anchoring it to the mission it must never fail.

Treating power as a mission-essential function keeps every design choice honest by tying it to the operation it must never fail. The availability gate sets how much redundancy assurance requires; the fuel gate sets a supply dependency to cover with sovereign sources and buffers; the plug and regime gates keep the burner at the design stage, so present missions rely on proven sources with fusion as the future anchor.

title: Scalability Across Installations
lede: A fleet of standardised burner units across many installations improves reliability growth and supply resilience, but multiplies the fuel demand.
body: From one unit to a fleet

Resilient sovereign power at scale means many installations, each with several units. A fleet of standardised units brings benefits — shared spares, faster reliability growth, common training — and one dominant challenge: fuel demand multiplies with every unit.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Scaling effects" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Standard unit</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">common design</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fleet</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">shared spares</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Reliability growth</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">FOAK to BOAK</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fuel demand</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">multiplies</text></svg>
Standardisation speeds reliability growth from FOAK toward BOAK availability.
Common spares and training improve MTTR across the fleet.
A fleet supports the redundancy that installation continuity requires.
The fuel constraint dominates at scale

Every added unit adds helium-3 demand, and one commercial unit already needs ~400× domestic supply. A fleet is therefore only conceivable with a fuel supply that scales — breeder-bred helium-3 domestically and, for true fleet scale, lunar helium-3. Scalability of the machines is meaningless without scalability of the fuel.

The honest scaling picture: the engineering benefits of a fleet are real and reinforce resilience, but the binding constraint is fuel supply. Scaling resilient sovereign power is as much a fuel-production programme (breeder, then lunar) as a machine-manufacturing programme — which is why the breeder is the foundation of the whole strategy.
Fuel is the binding constraint at scale

A fleet of standardised units speeds reliability growth and shares spares and training, reinforcing installation-level redundancy. But every added unit adds helium-3 demand on top of a per-unit requirement already ~400× domestic supply, so fleet scale is inconceivable without a fuel supply that scales — breeder-bred, then lunar. Scaling the machines is meaningless without scaling the fuel.

title: Interoperability with Existing Base Power
lede: A fusion unit must integrate with an installation's existing generation, distribution, and controls rather than requiring a wholesale rebuild.
body: Installations already have power systems: distribution, backup generators, storage, and controls. A fusion unit must interoperate with them — connecting to the existing bus, coordinating with existing sources, and speaking the existing control protocols — so it can be added incrementally rather than requiring a full rebuild.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Integration points" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion unit</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">new source</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Common bus</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">existing</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Controls</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">coordinated</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Existing sources</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">backup + storage</text></svg>
Electrical compatibility with the installation's distribution voltage and standards.
Control integration so the microgrid controller dispatches all sources together.
Protection coordination so faults are cleared consistently across old and new.
Physical integration of shielding, cooling, and fuel handling into the site.

Adding fusion as one more dispatchable source — anchoring base load while existing generators become backup — lets an installation improve resilience without a risky wholesale conversion. It also fits the redundancy story: the existing generators become part of the N+1 backup layer that the availability gate requires.

Interoperability is standard integration engineering, but it is essential to a realistic deployment concept. Resilient sovereign power is introduced by strengthening an installation's existing architecture, not by demanding it be discarded — a design-stage principle for a machine still working through its physics gates.

A fusion unit must connect to an installation's existing bus, coordinate with existing sources through the microgrid controller, and share fault-clearing behaviour, so it can be added as one more dispatchable source rather than through a risky wholesale conversion. The existing generators then become part of the N+1 backup layer the availability gate requires.

title: Operator Training and Human Factors
lede: A novel high-field machine needs trained operators and human-factored controls; skilled people are a resilience factor, not an afterthought.
body: A resilient installation depends on people as much as hardware. Operating and maintaining a high-field fusion unit — with its cryogenics, plasma control, and safety systems — requires trained operators and maintainers. A shortage of skilled people is itself a single point of failure that undermines availability and safety.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Human factors" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Trained operators</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Clear procedures</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Human-factored controls</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Safety culture</text></svg>
What training and human factors cover
Normal operation, start-up, and controlled shutdown of the machine.
Fault response, black-start, and restoration procedures.
Safe handling of helium-3/tritium inventory and activated materials.
Human-factored control interfaces that reduce error under stress.

Availability (0.86–0.995) and MTTR depend directly on operator and maintainer skill: fast, correct diagnosis and repair shorten downtime. Safety of a machine with high fields, cryogens, and a neutron fraction depends on disciplined procedures and a strong safety culture. Human factors are therefore a genuine lever on the honest reliability figures.

As a design-stage machine, the burner's training programme is a future task, but designing for maintainability and operability now — clear interfaces, modular access, good procedures — is part of building a machine that can actually deliver resilient power. People are the layer that makes the rest of the architecture work.

Availability and repair time depend directly on operator and maintainer skill, and safety of a high-field, cryogenic, neutron-producing machine depends on disciplined procedures and a strong safety culture. A shortage of skilled people is itself a single point of failure. Designing now for maintainability and operability — clear interfaces, modular access, good procedures — is part of building a machine that can deliver resilient power.

title: Safety and Fail-Safe Design
lede: A fusion installation near people must be designed to fail safe, with no possibility of runaway and controlled management of its neutron and fuel hazards.
body: Fusion has an inherent safety advantage: the reaction is not a chain reaction and cannot run away — loss of confinement or fuel simply stops fusion. On top of that inherent property, the installation is engineered to fail safe: any fault drives the machine toward a safe, shut-down state, protecting people and mission.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Fail-safe path" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fault</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">detected</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Safe response</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">controlled shutdown</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Contain</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fuel + activation</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Protect</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">people + mission</text></svg>
Neutron exposure from the 5.44% fraction — managed by shielding and interlocks.
Helium-3/tritium inventory — managed by containment and accountancy.
High magnetic fields and stored magnet energy — managed by protection systems.
Cryogenic hazards — managed by standard cryogenic safety practice.

A machine that fails safe protects both people and the rest of the installation: a fault trips the unit cleanly rather than damaging it or endangering personnel, and the redundant architecture carries the mission while it recovers. Fail-safe design and the availability gate work together — a clean trip is a recoverable trip.

Safety is stated honestly: fusion's inherent no-runaway property is a real advantage, but the neutron, fuel, magnetic, and cryogenic hazards are real and require engineered management. A safe design is a precondition for siting resilient power near people at a defense installation.

Fusion cannot run away: loss of confinement or fuel simply stops the reaction. On top of that inherent property the installation is engineered so any fault drives the machine to a safe shut-down state, and the redundant architecture carries the mission while it recovers. The neutron, fuel, magnetic, and cryogenic hazards are real and managed; a clean trip is a recoverable trip.

title: Aegis and MetroVolt: One Machine, Two Housings
lede: Aegis (fixed defense installations) and MetroVolt (data centers) are two housings of the same burner, so defense benefits from broader development.
body: The burner is a single D–3He tandem-mirror design offered in two housings: Aegis for fixed defense installations and MetroVolt for data centers. The physics, gates, and core engineering are shared; the housings differ in hardening, siting, and integration for their respective missions.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Shared machine" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Burner core</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">D-3He tandem mirror</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Aegis</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fixed defense sites</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">MetroVolt</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">data centers</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Shared gates</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">plug / regime / fuel</text></svg>
Why the shared design matters for defense
Development effort on the shared core benefits both applications.
Reliability growth in one housing informs the other.
A common machine supports a broader supply base and spares pool.

Aegis emphasises survivability, hardening, low signature, and sovereign fuel for contested and remote sites. MetroVolt emphasises the continuous, high-quality power a data center demands. The availability gate is stated identically for both (0.86–0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982), and it is the same honest figure whether the customer is a base or a data center.

The shared-machine structure is a strength: defense does not carry the whole development burden alone, and lessons transfer between housings. But the shared gates are shared honestly — the plug-stress, regime, fuel, and availability problems apply to Aegis and MetroVolt alike, because they are the same machine.

Because Aegis and MetroVolt are one machine in two housings, development effort and reliability growth in either benefit both, and a common design supports a broader supply base. The same availability figure (0.86–0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982) and the same plug, regime, and fuel gates apply to both housings, because they are the same machine — the merits are shared and so, honestly, are the obstacles.

title: Data-Center Crossover Lessons
lede: The hyperscale data-center reliability standard that defines the availability gate also offers proven techniques defense power can borrow.
body: The Tier III reference, and what it teaches

The availability gate is stated against the hyperscale data-center reference, Tier III 0.99982. That world has spent decades engineering extreme availability from imperfect components — and the techniques it developed transfer directly to resilient defense power.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Borrowed techniques" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Redundant sources</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">N+1 / 2N</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">No-break transfer</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">UPS + storage</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fault isolation</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">zoned design</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Concurrent maint.</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">service while running</text></svg>
Concurrent maintainability: service any element without dropping load.
No-break power: storage-backed transfer so loads never see a switch.
Redundancy topologies: N+1, N+2, and 2N proven at scale.
Rigorous availability accounting and testing discipline.
Why it does not close the gap by itself

These techniques are how a system of 0.86–0.995 units reaches toward 0.99982 at the installation level. But data centers achieve their figures with mature, fielded generation; the burner is a design-stage source. Borrowing the architecture helps close the gap; it does not remove the fact that the fusion unit itself is not yet built or proven.

The crossover is genuine and useful: the same MetroVolt housing serves data centers, so the reliability engineering developed there flows back to Aegis. Defense benefits from a discipline honed in the most availability-demanding commercial environment, applied honestly to a machine still working through its gates.
Borrowed discipline, not a closed gap

Concurrent maintainability, no-break transfer, proven redundancy topologies, and rigorous availability accounting from the hyperscale world are how a system of 0.86–0.995 units reaches toward 0.99982 at the installation level. But data centers achieve their figures with mature, fielded generation; borrowing the architecture helps close the gap without removing the fact that the burner is a design-stage source.

title: What Net Gain Means for Power
lede: A machine can produce fusion power without producing net electricity; the honest distinction matters for any resilient-power claim.
body: Fusion power is not net electricity

It is easy to conflate a machine that fuses with a machine that delivers net electricity to a base. They are different. The breeder's design point is a scientific gain Q_sci of 3.424 at 88.7 MW of fusion power — a gain measure, not a statement that the machine powers a base. There is no hardware net-gain claim before FOAK.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Gain to power" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Q_sci 3.424</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">scientific gain</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion power</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">88.7 MW</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Engineering losses</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">subtract</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Net electricity</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">the real test</text></svg>
The chain from gain to delivered power
Scientific gain (Q_sci) compares fusion power to heating power in the plasma.
Engineering gain accounts for the whole plant's power draw — magnets, cryogenics, systems.
Net electricity is what remains for the base after all plant loads.
Availability then determines how much of the time that net power is delivered.
Why this candor matters for defense

A resilient-power claim must rest on net delivered electricity at high availability, not on a scientific gain figure. Kronos uses the frozen design numbers exactly and does not translate a Q_sci of 3.424 into a delivered-power promise. The burner's own net-power case is subject to its plug, regime, and fuel gates, none closed today.

The honest statement: these machines are design-and-simulation studies aiming at net power, with a defined first hardware step at breeder FOAK (~2030). Net gain in hardware is a milestone ahead, not a present fact — and resilient sovereign power depends on reaching it.
Delivered power is the real test

A resilient-power claim must rest on net delivered electricity at high availability, not on a scientific gain figure. Kronos uses the frozen design numbers exactly — Q_sci 3.424 at 88.7 MW for the breeder — and does not translate a gain measure into a delivered-power promise. Net gain in hardware is a milestone at breeder FOAK (~2030), not a present fact, and resilient sovereign power depends on reaching it.

title: Power for Command and Control
lede: Command and control nodes are the highest-priority loads on a base microgrid and are protected by dedicated conditioning, storage, and redundancy.
body: Command and control (C2) — the systems that direct the mission — are the loads that must never lose power. On a base microgrid, C2 sits at the top of the load-priority hierarchy: everything else can be shed to protect it, and it receives the most redundancy and the cleanest power.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Protecting C2" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Sources</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fusion + storage</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">No-break bus</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">UPS</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Priority tier</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">C2 first</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Load shed</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">below C2</text></svg>
A dedicated uninterruptible bus so C2 never sees a source transition.
Highest priority in dispatch and load-shedding logic.
Power conditioning for the clean, stable supply sensitive electronics need.

Because the burner can trip (0.86–0.995 availability), C2 is deliberately insulated from the fusion unit's behaviour: storage carries C2 through any transition, and redundant sources back it. C2 continuity is engineered to be independent of whether any single generator is up — exactly the discipline the availability gate demands.

Protecting C2 is where the whole resilient-power architecture proves itself. If command and control stay powered through grid loss, fuel interruption, a unit trip, and maintenance, the installation has achieved continuity where it matters most — and it does so through layered redundancy, not through any claim that the fusion unit alone is continuous.

C2 is deliberately insulated from the fusion unit's behaviour by a dedicated uninterruptible bus and redundant feeds, so its continuity is independent of whether any single generator is up — exactly the discipline the availability gate demands.

title: Reducing the Attack Surface of Power
lede: On-site generation removes the fuel convoy and grid tie as attack surfaces, while adding a fixed installation and a fuel chain that must be defended.
body: The attack surface of a power system is everything an adversary can target to deny power: the grid, fuel convoys, storage, the plant, controls, and supply chains. Reducing it means removing dependencies an adversary can exploit — and honestly accounting for the new ones any change introduces.

The commercial grid as a shared, external dependency.
The continuous fuel convoy as a repeatedly targetable movement.
Large forward fuel storage as a fixed target.
A fixed, locatable generating installation to defend.
A helium-3 supply and refuelling chain to secure.
A cyber-physical control system to protect.

The net effect is favourable but not absolute: the largest, most frequently exposed surfaces (grid, convoy) shrink, while the added surfaces (fixed plant, small fuel chain, controls) are fewer, more concentrated, and easier to harden and defend. Reducing the attack surface is a real benefit of sovereign power, stated with its trade-offs rather than as an unqualified win.

On-site fusion removes the largest, most frequently exposed surfaces — the grid and the recurring convoy — while adding a fixed plant, a small fuel chain, and a control system. The added surfaces are fewer, more concentrated, and easier to harden and defend. The net effect is favourable but not absolute, and it is stated with its trade-offs rather than as an unqualified win.

title: Independence Duration and Fuel Interval
lede: How long a base can run with no external supply is set largely by its on-site fuel interval, a key resilience metric for the burner.
body: Independence duration is how long an installation can sustain mission power with no external input — no grid, no resupply. For a fuel-fed base it is short, set by fuel storage and consumption. For a burner it is potentially long, set by the energy density of its helium-3 charge and its steady operation.

D–<sup>3</sup>He is energy-dense: a small fuel mass carries a large amount of energy.
Steady base-load operation means predictable, efficient fuel use.
A compact charge is easier to stockpile on-site than bulk liquid fuel.

Independence duration is bounded by two things beyond fuel: availability and non-fuel dependencies. A long fuel interval does not help if the unit is down (availability 0.86–0.995), so redundancy still matters. And the fuel charge must be filled from a sovereign supply that, at ~400× demand, does not yet exist at scale — so independence duration is a design property waiting on the fuel pathway.

Independence duration is one of the burner's most attractive resilience properties: a base that runs for a long interval on a compact, stockpilable charge is far less hostage to its supply lines. Stated honestly, it is a genuine advantage conditioned on availability and on a sovereign fuel supply being real.

It is bounded by availability, since a long fuel interval does not help while a unit is down, and by the sovereign supply that must fill the charge. Independence duration is a real advantage conditioned on the availability and fuel gates.

title: Power Density and Footprint
lede: A compact high-output source with direct energy conversion can reduce the physical footprint of installation power, within siting and shielding limits.
body: On a defense installation, space is a resource: a smaller footprint for power generation leaves more room for the mission, simplifies hardening, and reduces the area that must be defended. Power density — output per unit footprint — is therefore a meaningful design property.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Footprint drivers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Compact core</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">high field</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Direct conversion</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">no big steam plant</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Shielding</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">5.44% neutrons</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Redundancy</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">multiple units</text></svg>
Direct energy conversion removes a large steam-cycle and cooling island.
A high-field tandem mirror is compact for its output.
A long fuel interval removes large on-site fuel storage.

Compactness is offset by shielding (the 5.44% neutron fraction needs a shielding boundary), by cryogenic and control plant, and above all by redundancy: an installation carries multiple separated units to meet the availability gate, plus storage. The system footprint is larger than a single unit, though still favourable versus the fuel storage and generation a comparable fuel-fed base needs.

Power density is a real design merit, presented with its offsets. The honest picture is a compact core whose system footprint is driven up by the shielding and redundancy that safety and the availability gate require — net favourable, but not the footprint of the bare machine.

Direct energy conversion and a high-field core make the machine compact for its output and remove large fuel storage, but shielding, cryogenic and control plant, and above all redundancy raise the system footprint. The honest picture is a compact core whose system footprint is driven up by the shielding and redundancy that safety and the availability gate require — net favourable, but not the footprint of the bare machine.

title: Grid Support and Export When Available
lede: An installation that generates its own power can also support or export to the surrounding grid when it is healthy, adding regional resilience.
body: Sovereign power is usually framed as independence from the grid, but the relationship can be two-way. When the commercial grid is healthy, an installation with surplus generation can support or export to it, strengthening regional resilience — and when the grid fails, the installation islands and carries itself.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Two-way tie" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Base generation</text><text x="85" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">surplus</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Grid tie</text><text x="269" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">export when healthy</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Grid stress</text><text x="453" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">support</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637" y="49" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Grid loss</text><text x="637" y="67" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">island</text></svg>
During normal grid operation, surplus base power can supplement the local grid.
During grid stress, the installation can provide stabilising support.
During grid loss, the installation disconnects and runs islanded.

Export is a benefit only when there is genuine surplus, and mission power always has priority: the installation never exports at the expense of its own continuity. And with availability at 0.86–0.995, the base cannot be counted on as a firm grid resource without its own redundancy. Export is opportunistic support, not a committed grid service.

This capability adds value beyond the fence line — a resilient installation can be a good neighbour to the regional grid — while the sovereignty and continuity of the mission remain the first priority. It is presented as an option enabled by on-site generation, bounded by the same honest availability figure that governs everything else.

title: Resilient Power Design Principles
lede: A short set of principles governs how Kronos designs resilient sovereign power: layered redundancy, honest availability, sovereign fuel, and fail-safe operation.
body: Across every page in this section, the same design principles recur. Stated together, they define how Kronos approaches resilient sovereign power for fixed defense installations — and each is grounded in a physics or engineering reality, not a marketing aim.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 300" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Design principles" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="130" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="1.00"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="97" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.92"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="63" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.84"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="30" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5" opacity="0.76"/><circle cx="380" cy="40" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="44" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Sovereign fuel</text><circle cx="380" cy="70" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="74" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Layered redundancy</text><circle cx="380" cy="100" r="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="104" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Honest availability</text><circle cx="380" cy="130" r="6" fill="#2E3947" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="396" y="134" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Fail-safe operation</text></svg>
Never a sole source: the fusion unit is an anchor in a redundant system, because availability is 0.86–0.995, not 0.99982.
Design to the honest number: size redundancy and storage to the availability we can defend, not to an aspirational figure.
Sovereign fuel or no claim: resilient power requires breeder-bred and, later, lunar helium-3, given the ~400× supply gate.
Fail safe: every fault drives the machine to a safe state; a clean trip is a recoverable trip.
Layered survivability: siting, hardening, separation, and redundancy together, not any one alone.
Why the principles are the product

The burner is a design-stage machine with open gates. What Kronos can offer today is not fielded hardware but a disciplined, honest way of designing toward resilient sovereign power — principles that hold whether the anchor source is the burner tomorrow or a proven source in the interim.

These principles keep the resilient-power story truthful: significant promise, named obstacles, and an architecture built around the real behaviour of the machine rather than around the behaviour anyone might wish it had.
